In 1763, France had a choice: keep Canada, or keep two small Caribbean sugar islands.

It chose the sugar islands.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ By 1762, Britain had captured Quebec, Montreal, Martinique, Guadeloupe, plus Spain's Havana and Manila. At the peace table, France's negotiator got to pick some of it back. He picked Guadeloupe and Martinique.

2/ The logic was cold arithmetic. Sugar from those two islands, grown on enslaved labor, was worth more to France by contemporary estimates than everything Canada's fur trade brought in. Canada, commercially, was the smaller prize.

3/ Voltaire had already mocked the whole war in Candide (1759), having a character sneer that France and Britain were spending more fighting over Canada — "a few acres of snow" — than the place was worth. It landed because many agreed.

4/ Britain had its own version of this debate. Some, including wartime leader William Pitt, argued for taking the profitable sugar islands instead of Canada. Britain kept Canada anyway — for strategic reasons, not commercial ones.

5/ Spain's piece: it got Havana and Manila back, ceded Florida as the price, and had already been secretly handed French Louisiana west of the Mississippi the year before, as compensation. Three continents, one signature, 10 Feb 1763.

6/ With France gone from eastern North America, Britain no longer needed 13 colonies to help fund their own defense against a rival empire. The taxes London kept collecting anyway became a grievance. That's a straight line to 1776.
